chief_complaint: severe crampy pelvic pain during first 2 days of periods
hpi_details: A 17-year-old female presents with recurrent severe crampy pelvic pain during the first 2 days of her periods, without symptoms between menses.
ideas: She thinks she might have cysts in her ovaries like her older sister had as a teenager.
concerns: She is worried that missing several days of school every month will cause her to fall behind and fail her upcoming midterms.
expectations: She hopes to get a prescription for stronger pain medication and a doctor's note for her physical education teacher.
social_hx: No tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary dysmenorrhea is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Primary Dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen/Naproxen) started 1-2 days before menses, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe crampy pelvic pain during first 2 days of periods
Key HPI features: A 17-year-old female has recurrent severe crampy pelvic pain during the first 2 days of her periods, without symptoms between menses.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Dysmenorrhea.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary dysmenorrhea.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Endometriosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring warning signs of secondary dysmenorrhea, including progressively worsening pain, pain outside menses, or heavy/irregular bleeding.
management_principles: Plan for Primary Dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen/Naproxen) started 1-2 days before menses
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Patient with severe crampy pelvic pain during the first 2 days of her period.
red_flags: Progressively worsening pain, pain outside menses, or heavy/irregular bleeding may indicate secondary dysmenorrhea

must_ask.objective: Characterize the timing of pain relative to menses
must_ask.say: Does the pain start right when your period begins, and how long does it last?

must_ask.objective: Screen for symptoms outside of menses
must_ask.say: Do you have pelvic pain at other times of the month, or only during your period?
Have you tried ibuprofen or similar medication, and does it help?
Is there any chance you could be pregnant?

must_ask.objective: Screen for red flags of secondary dysmenorrhea
must_ask.say: Is the pain getting worse over time, or is it the same each cycle?
Starting ibuprofen or naproxen 1-2 days before your period begins can help significantly.

history.answer: I came in because I get severe crampy pain in my lower belly during the first two days of my period.
The cramps started about a year after my very first period, around when I was 13 or 14, and I have had them with almost every cycle since.
The pain starts right when my period begins and lasts through the first two days. Outside of those two days, I have no symptoms at all.
It is a severe, crampy ache right in the center of my lower belly above my pubic bone. It often radiates into my lower back and inner thighs.
On the first two days it reaches an 8 out of 10. It is so bad that I usually have to stay in bed with a heating pad and miss school.
No, the severity has stayed pretty consistent from month to month rather than getting steadily worse over the years.
I usually wait until the cramps are unbearable and take a regular Tylenol, but it barely does anything. I have never tried taking ibuprofen or naproxen regularly before the pain starts.
I feel nauseated and have loose bowel movements on the first day, and sometimes a dull headache, but I do not throw up.
My bleeding lasts about four to five days and is normal in amount. I do not pass large blood clots, and I never bleed or spot between periods.
I have never been sexually active, so I have never experienced that.
No, I do not have pain when urinating or having bowel movements, other than the loose stools on the first day.
history.topic: Pain with urination or bowel movements

history.answer: No, I have not had any fever, chills, or unusual discharge down there.
No, it has never been a sudden sharp pain on just one side, and I have never felt dizzy or fainted.
My first period was when I was 12 years old. My periods come regularly every 28 to 30 days.
My last period started about two weeks ago, so I am right in the middle of my cycle and feel completely fine today.
I have never had sex, and I have never had any sexually transmitted infections.
I am not taking birth control pills, and I do not have an intrauterine device.
There is no chance that I could be pregnant because I have never had sex.
My mother told me she also had severe period cramps when she was a teenager, but no one in my family has endometriosis or fibroids.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions or health problems.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never stayed in a hospital.
I do not take any daily prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I do not smoke, vape, drink alcohol, or use any recreational drugs.
I am a high school student and I live at home with my parents.
My older sister had terrible cramps from ovarian cysts when she was my age, so I wondered if I might have them too.
I've already missed three days of classes this month and I'm really worried I'm going to fall behind and fail my exams.
I was hoping you could give me stronger pain medication that actually works and a medical note for my gym teacher.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-nourished, comfortable adolescent female in no acute distress.
Conjunctivae pink without pallor; sclerae anicteric.
Abdomen flat and symmetrical with no distension, rashes, or surgical scars.
Normal active bowel sounds present in all four quadrants.
Soft, non-tender to light and deep palpation throughout; no suprapubic tenderness or palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary guarding.
Normal female external genitalia with no discharge or lesions; internal examination deferred given patient has never been sexually active.
